Commentary.Commentary: We are all set to get the chase underway in an increasingly dark and overcast sky, which could offer crucial swing and seam movement for the bowling side. Sri Lankan openers Chamari Athapaththu and Vishmi Gunarathne have taken guard in the middle, heavily aware that a strong Powerplay is essential to hunting down the target of 151. Tasked with stopping them is right-arm medium-pacer Rosemary Mair, who takes the new ball for the White Ferns and will look to exploit the cloud cover to capture an immediate, vital breakthrough for New Zealand. Let's go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

An exciting chase ahead - While a target of 151 is far from insurmountable, it will require a clinical and sustained batting effort from Sri Lanka to complete the chase. The pitch conditions and the scoreboard pressure mean the Lankans cannot afford a sluggish start or lose wickets. Facing a potent and highly experienced New Zealand bowling lineup, the Sri Lankan top order must bat with intent and maturity to pull off a victory. Join us in a bit for Sri Lanka Women's reply.

A quick chat - New Zealand Women's Sophie Devine is up for a flash interview. She admits that they are hugely disappointed despite working so hard in the middle, and reckons they are around 20 runs short. On the pitch, Devine says it played a touch slower than the previous match at the same venue. She credits the Sri Lankan bowlers for keeping things tight and hitting the stumps consistently, adding that it has given New Zealand a clear blueprint to follow with the ball. She is quick to add, though, that executing it will still take a strong bowling performance. On moving forward, Devine says the past cannot be controlled and the only thing that matters now is the next moment.

Mid-innings recovery - The innings stabilized and gained momentum thanks to a crucial partnership between Amelia Kerr and Sophie Devine, who both anchored the team with matching scores of 45 before being dismissed. Their departures stall the scoring, restricting New Zealand to the 150-mark. Sri Lanka's bowling attack maintained a disciplined display throughout the innings, headlined by Kavisha Dilhari, who claimed two scalps, while the rest of the unit chipped in with tidy, restrictive spells.

White Ferns post under-par total - New Zealand Women finished their 20 overs at 150/6, a score they likely consider a shade under-par relative to their expectations. Despite falling slightly short of a truly commanding target, the Kiwis will remain confident in their ability to defend it, given the sheer quality of their bowling unit. After electing to bat first, the White Ferns struggled to find their rhythm early on, scratching together just 38 runs during the initial 6-over Powerplay while losing a crucial early wicket.

Wonderful bowling in the death phase by the Lankans! New Zealand Women finish on 150/6. Shade fuller on off, Jess Kerr scuffs it to the mid off region and they hustle for the single, but will have to settle for just one only. Just 7 runs off the final over.

Amelia Kerr has a lot of responsibility on her shoulders and will need to anchor this innings, while Sophie Devine's role in the middle order becomes a lot more crucial with the current situation of the game. Skipper Chamari Athapaththu brings herself into the attack after the break.

FOUR! Top shot! Length ball, around the off stump line. Plimmer jumps out of her crease and drills it down the ground, to mid off's right, for a boundary. New Zealand Women end their Powerplay with 38/1 on the board.

Commentary.Commentary: Not the start the White Ferns wanted. Sri Lanka have their tails up. In walks the captain, Amelia Kerr, at number 3.

OUT! EDGED AND GONE! That is a superb catch from the keeper. Mithali Ayodhya lands this on a good length and in the channel outside off, gets it to move away again. Isabella Gaze, without moving her feet, wafts at it away from her body. Gets a thin outside edge to the right of the keeper, with the ball dying down. Kaushini Nuthyangana gets low sharply and scoops the ball into her gloves just above the ground. The finger is raised on the appeal, and Gaze is on her way to the dugout, but she is stopped as the umpires have sent it for a review. There's a clear edge, and the keeper's gloves are well under the ball. A clean catch and Gaze departs. New Zealand Women are 4/1 now.
Commentary.Howout: c Kaushini Nuthyangana b Mithali Ayodhya
Commentary.Default_Commentary: 0.3: Mithali Ayodhya to Isabella Gaze, OUT! c Kaushini Nuthyangana b Mithali Ayodhya.

Commentary.Commentary: Is Gaze caught behind? Well, the umpire has given out but has gone upstairs to be doubly sure. There's no doubt about the edge. And it's deemed a clean catch after a couple of replays are checked. Gaze falls. OUT!

FOUR! New Zealand Women are underway in style! Mithali Ayodhya goes for the yorker but ends up serving a low full toss, on middle and leg. Isabella Gaze shows the full face of the bat and drives it down the ground to the left of mid on for the first boundary of the game.
Commentary.Default_Commentary: 0.2: Mithali Ayodhya to Isabella Gaze, Four!

Commentary.Default_Commentary: 0.1: Mithali Ayodhya to Isabella Gaze, No run.

Commentary.Commentary: Time to play - Done with all the pre-match rituals. Sri Lanka Matha and God Defend New Zealand are both sung/chanted proudly. We are all set for the game to get underway in Southampton. The crowd is gradually building up at the venue and the conditions are bright as of now. Out walk the two umpires. Chamari Athapaththu has her ladies in a huddle near the ropes. Now, they spring out and spread to their fielding spots. Georgia Plimmer and Isabella Gaze are the two Kiwi openers who walk to the crease. New Zealand have gone with the same team and have trusted this group. The slingy pacer, Mithali Ayodhya, is all set to bowl the first over. Gaze to face. A slip in place. 3... 2... 1 and off we go!

Time for the national anthems - The giant flags of both countries are unfurled in the middle. Out walk the match officials and right after them, the two captains lead their respective groups out and get lined up. It will be the national anthem of Sri Lanka first, followed by New Zealand's.

Hasini Perera, Sri Lanka Women, is next for a quick talk - On the team's response following the opening defeat, Hasini says the squad came together to reflect on what went wrong and used the two days of practice to work on individual areas. She adds that the hope now is to take that preparation and execute it out in the middle. On working with the new head coach, Perera shares that the atmosphere in the dugout has been positive and straightforward. She notes that he keeps things simple and clear, making it easy for the players to understand their roles and back their plans. On her own batting form, Perera highlights that the last five to six months have been encouraging, but she is putting all of that aside as she heads into this tournament with a fresh mindset.

Maddy Green, New Zealand Women, is up for a chat - When asked about what the chat was like after the loss, Maddy says it was a disappointing result for them and one the team is keen to put behind them quickly. She notes the side felt they had posted a competitive total on that surface and that the bowling, for the most part, was disciplined enough to create opportunities. She admits that the dropped chances hurt, particularly for a side that takes pride in its fielding standards. Adds that the preparation and work ethic have never been in question, but the challenge now is putting everything together when it matters. On bouncing back, Green stresses that the focus now is on remaining calm and backing their skills under pressure. She details that the preparation and practice levels in camp have not dropped, and that the group simply needs to convert that work into execution when it counts. On her own development as a batter, Green underlines that the last few years have been about expanding her shot selection and being more expressive at the crease. She adds that the number six position feels increasingly like her own, and her goal now is to own that role and finish games for New Zealand.

PITCH REPORT - Ian Smith is pitchside with his assessment of the conditions. He mentions the same pitch will be used from the last game. Mentions that the square boundaries are 63 and 65 meters respectively, with the straight hit being 72 meters. Ebony-Rainford Brent joins him and says that the pitch looks absolutely brilliant. Adds that 163 was scored in the last game, and we will more or less see something similar. Shares that whenever the bowlers went short or overpitched, they got punished. Says that Alleyene of West Indies had a lot of success bowling a bit full, and batters mistimed their shots down the ground, which could be something the bowlers will look to use again in this game.

The captain of Sri Lanka Women - Chamari Athapaththu says they would have bowled first. On how quickly they have adjusted to the conditions, she admits that it is not easy, but as professional players, they have to adapt. About the team combination, she informs that they are going with three changes in the team. On being asked about what the key areas of improvement are from the previous game, Chamari straight up says that they need to improve their bowling and bowl better lines and lengths.

The captain of New Zealand Women - Amelia Kerr says that it is the same wicket as the other night, so they just want to put up runs on the board. Adds that the wicket may get a bit slower later on but still looks pretty good. Mentions that it was a very disappointing effort in the field in the last game. She thought they batted and bowled well, and if they took their chances, they would have won by probably 50 runs. Reckons that they have had a chat about that and will look to improve on it. Informs that they are unchanged.

Sri Lanka Women (Playing XI) - Chamari Athapaththu (C), Vishmi Gunarathne, Hasini Perera (In for Imesha Dulani), Harshitha Samarawickrama, Kavisha Dilhari, Nilakshika Silva, Kaushini Nuthyangana (WK), Sugandika Kumari, Kawya Kavindi (In for Hansima Karunaratne), Mithali Ayodhya and Nimasha Meepage (In for Malki Madara).

New Zealand Women (Unchanged Playing XI) - Isabella Gaze (WK), Georgia Plimmer, Amelia Kerr (C), Sophie Devine, Brooke Halliday, Maddy Green, Izzy Sharp, Jess Kerr, Nensi Patel, Rosemary Mair and Bree Illing.

TOSS - The sun is blazing out there, and both captains, Amelia Kerr and Chamari Athapaththu, are out in the middle. Nasser Hussain leads the proceedings. The coin flip lands in favor of the Kiwis. New Zealand Women have elected to BAT first.

Did you know? It’s been quite a while since Sri Lankans tasted success in the T20 World Cups. Of course, they are chasing their maiden title win, but more critically, they are on a seven-match losing streak in the global event, with their last win coming against Bangladesh in the 2023 edition. New Zealand, on the other hand, are yet to lose a game against the Islanders in the tournament, and will hope to continue this insane winning streak. However, on English soil, they have managed to win just two out of ten completed T20I matches, a record they would be keen to improve on. So with a lot riding on for the two teams, it promises to be a spicy contest in the making. Stay tuned as the toss and team sheets will flash up shortly.

Expected team combinations - New Zealand face a selection headache heading into this game. Suzie Bates, one of their most experienced campaigners and their leading run getter in T20 World Cups, with over 1200 runs, was left out of the opening match, making it the first time the White Ferns had played a Women's T20 World Cup game without her. Whether she comes back into the XI is the big question, though slotting her back in means reshuffling the batting order. Whereas if need be, Lea Tahuhu, another of their prolific players, might as well get swapped in to strengthen their bowling. Sri Lanka have their own selection puzzle to solve. They handed debuts to a couple of bowlers in their opener, while leaving out Hasini Perera, one of only five Sri Lankan batters to have crossed the 1000-run mark in T20 internationals. She could be slotted back if need be to strengthen the batting unit that has struggled badly.

As things stand - Group B has been blown wide open after just one round of matches. New Zealand were guilty of a shambolic fielding display against West Indies, dropping six or seven catches and looking a shade of the world champions they are at the beginning of their title defence. Sri Lanka were let down on both ends. The batting crumbled the moment Chamari Athapaththu failed to fire, exposing just how heavily this side leans on their captain. And with the ball, it was no better, as their bowling attack managed just a solitary wicket across their bowling effort and were torn apart. With the Kiwis still to face heavyweights England and the Islanders yet to take on West Indies as their next big challenges, both would want to grab two crucial points in this fixture. Both head into this game bruised and desperate to avoid a premature exit from the tournament.

No room for error - Two teams. Two humbling defeats to start their World Cup campaigns. Now, at The Hampshire Bowl, they stand face-to-face to resurrect their respective journey onto the correct path. With all teams playing their opening games, the action in the ICC Women’s T20 World Cup 2026 resumes after a day’s break. Hello and welcome to the exciting double header in Group B. It all starts with a very crucial clash, as New Zealand Women go up against Sri Lanka Women. It will then be followed by hosts England Women taking on their neighbours, Ireland Women, with both games scheduled to be played in Southampton. So let’s enjoy an action-packed day of cricket.
... MATCH DAY ...

Two ships in different storms - New Zealand arrive in England as the defending champions, having claimed their maiden T20 World Cup title in 2024, a golden crown they are now desperately trying to keep. Led by the imperious Amelia Kerr, the White Ferns carry a squad that blends the legend of the past with the hunger of the future. Veterans Suzie Bates and Sophie Devine are turning up for what will be their 10th and final T20 World Cup, determined to walk off the international stage with medals around their necks. But the fairytale beginning New Zealand had scripted in their minds was quickly torn up. The Windies handed them a 7-wicket defeat in their opening game at Southampton, which stunned the defending champions. On the other side of the ledger is Sri Lanka, a team that has never once made it beyond the group stage in the Women's T20 World Cup. Captained by Chamari Athapaththu, the Lankans too come into this contest wounded. England humiliated them in the opening game at Edgbaston, posting a record-breaking total, 219, the highest total in Women's T20 World Cup history, before Freya Kemp and her company bowled them out for 132. Two teams, both bruised, both burning for a first win. The Hampshire Bowl on June 16 is where one of them gets to breathe again. A record that says it all - If we talk about the history between the two giants, New Zealand hold an almost unfair advantage walking into this fixture. In 17 Women's T20I matches played between the two sides, New Zealand have won 14 of them, with Sri Lanka managing just two victories and one match being abandoned. What is even more striking is that, in every single T20 World Cup meeting between the two nations across seven encounters, New Zealand have emerged victorious every time. The White Ferns have essentially made this fixture their own private property in the biggest events. For Sri Lanka, snapping that streak wouldn't just be a win, it would be a statement that this is a different team, in a different era. The Chamari factor - When Sri Lanka wins a match, they have usually done so because one player stood impossibly tall. That player is almost always Chamari Athapaththu. She is the only Sri Lankan to have represented the nation in all nine previous editions of the Women's T20 World Cup, and at the age where most captains begin to wind down, Athapaththu only grows in consequence. Sri Lanka's batting revolves around her and when she fires, the whole team fires. Against England, Athapaththu fell cheaply for just 4, and the innings unravelled around that moment. New Zealand's bowlers will have a detailed plan for her, but containing the world's most destructive opener is far easier said than done. If Athapaththu finds her range at Southampton, Sri Lanka will be in this game for every single over. Team form (Last 5 completed Women’s T20Is, recent first) - NZ-W - LLWLW | SL-W - LWWWW. Towards the throne or the exit door - This is a match loaded with stakes that neither side can afford to ignore. For New Zealand, defeat will likely make things tougher for them and you simply cannot lose two in a row in a group of six with only the top two advancing. For Sri Lanka, another loss effectively shuts the door on that historic group stage breakthrough they have chased for over a decade. The head-to-head numbers scream New Zealand. But here in Southampton, where seam and swing might favour enterprising cricket, a motivated Sri Lanka side under their living legend Chamari Athapaththu can cause an upset that the Women's T20 World Cup will talk about for years. One team defends a crown. The other chases history. At the Hampshire Bowl, both will be fighting like they have nothing left to lose, because truthfully, they don't.
